Ambidextrous

am-bih-DEK-struhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ambidextrous is able to use both the right and left hand equally well.

Growing up ambidextrous, she never had to decide which hand to favor when learning to play tennis.

Worked Example

The famous painter trained himself to be ambidextrous later in life, switching brushes between hands whenever one arm grew tired.

He wasn't born naturally able to use both hands -- he deliberately built the skill, but the end result, equal comfort with either hand, is still what ambidextrous means.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — handy → ambidextrous → virtuosic

handy vs. ambidextrous

handy vs. ambidextrous: reasonably skillful, especially with tools or the hands

virtuosic vs. ambidextrous

virtuosic vs. ambidextrous: possessing extraordinary skill, especially in the arts

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of ambidextrous.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ambi-

prefix — ambi-: both (Latin)

root — dexter

root — dexter: right hand (and, by extension, skill) (Latin)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ambidextrous comes from Latin ambi- ('both') + dexter ('right hand,' also the source of skill-words like dexterity) + -ous ('full of') -- literally 'full of right-handedness on both sides,' or equally skilled with either hand.

Use the root in a new word: dexterity

Use the root in a new word: dexterity: The magician's dexterity with a deck of cards amazed the children in the front row.

Word Choice

Ambidextrous describes genuine, trained equal skill with both hands -- don't use it loosely for someone who is just generally good at many things.
